text: The 33⅓ rpm vinyl record was introduced in 1948: for the first time almost half an hour of music fitted on each side.
The first radio broadcast with music and speech is credited to Reginald Fessenden, on Christmas Eve 1906, from Massachusetts.
A compact disc is 12 centimetres wide and, according to the Philips and Sony legend, its 74 minutes were chosen so Beethoven's Ninth would fit.
The piano was originally called "gravicembalo col piano e forte": a harpsichord that could play soft and loud depending on the touch.
Concert pitch sets middle A at 440 hertz under an international standard from 1955, although many orchestras tune slightly higher.
A classical guitar has six strings, but the baroque guitar had five courses of doubled strings.
The mechanical metronome was patented by Johann Maelzel in 1815, and Beethoven was among the first composers to mark his tempos with it.
The word "jazz" first appeared in print in Californian sports pages around 1912, before it named the music.
A Stradivarius violin is made of more than 70 pieces of wood, mainly spruce for the top and maple for the back.
FM radio was invented to cut interference: Edwin Armstrong demonstrated it in public in 1935.
The MP3 format was developed at Germany's Fraunhofer institute, and the ".mp3" extension was chosen in 1995.
The shortest song ever to enter the UK charts lasts under two seconds: "You Suffer" by Napalm Death.
The organ in the church of Halberstadt, Germany, is playing a John Cage piece meant to last 639 years; the chords change every few years.
A young human ear hears roughly 20 to 20,000 hertz; the lowest note on a grand piano is about 27 hertz.
Philips introduced the compact cassette in 1963 and chose not to charge licence fees for it, which made it a worldwide standard.
Beethoven's Ninth was the first major symphony to include a choir and vocal soloists.
The theremin is played without touching it: two antennas sense the distance of the hands to control pitch and volume.
The oldest hymn with surviving written music is the Hymn to Nikkal, found at Ugarit and dated to around 1400 BC.
The oldest licensed commercial radio station in the United States, KDKA in Pittsburgh, began broadcasting in November 1920.
A C major chord is made of three notes: C, E and G.
The Moog synthesizer of 1964 was one of the first voltage-controlled electronic instruments with a keyboard.
A vibraphone has a motor that spins discs inside its tubes to produce its characteristic vibrato.
John Cage's "4′33″" contains no notes at all: the performer stays silent for four minutes and thirty-three seconds.
The five-note pentatonic scale appears in traditional music all over the world, from China to Scotland.
Opera was born in Florence at the end of the 16th century; Jacopo Peri's "Dafne" of 1598 is considered the first.
The Motown label takes its name from "Motor Town", the nickname of Detroit, where it was founded in 1959.
A guitar string vibrating twice as fast sounds one octave higher.
Sony's Walkman went on sale in Japan in July 1979 and made listening to music anywhere with headphones popular.
The accordion was patented in Vienna in 1829, and today it is a national instrument in places as different as Argentina and Colombia.
DAB digital radio carries several stations in one multiplex, which is why one frequency can hold many stations.
The double bass is the largest and lowest bowed string instrument in the orchestra, and it is also plucked in jazz.
The most used drum sample in history is the "Amen break", six seconds from a 1969 track by The Winstons.
The Eurovision Song Contest was first held in 1956 in Lugano, Switzerland, with seven countries.
The oldest known flute is about 40,000 years old and was made from a vulture bone, in a cave in Germany.
The tuning fork, the metal fork that gives the reference note, was invented by the trumpeter John Shore in 1711.
Ravel's "Boléro" repeats the same melody for about fifteen minutes, changing only the orchestration and the volume.
The solid-body electric guitar became popular in the 1950s with models such as the Telecaster and the Les Paul.
A 12-inch vinyl record spins at 33⅓ rpm, and the stylus travels almost half a kilometre of groove per side.
Tango was declared Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2009, proposed by Argentina and Uruguay.
Flamenco has also been Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity since 2010.
The earliest surviving sound recording dates from 1860: a phonautograph captured a few seconds of "Au clair de la lune".
Edison's phonograph of 1877 recorded on tinfoil cylinders; flat discs arrived a decade later with Berliner.
A saxophone is made of metal, but it is classed as a woodwind because it sounds with a reed.
A four-part choir is usually divided into soprano, alto, tenor and bass, hence the abbreviation SATB.
Stereo vinyl records went on sale in 1958: each wall of the groove carries one channel.
Beethoven's "Ode to Joy" has been the official anthem of the European Union since 1985, without lyrics.
The ukulele was born in Hawaii at the end of the 19th century from Portuguese instruments brought by emigrants from Madeira.
Early 20th-century crystal radios worked without batteries: the radio signal itself provided the power.
A tempo of 120 beats per minute is the most common in dance music, close to the pace of a brisk march.
The oldest complete song with notation is the Seikilos epitaph, carved on a Greek stele around the 1st century.
The world's largest carillon has 77 bells and stands in New York; it is played with fists and feet from a keyboard.
The harmonica was originally tuned to a single key; blues players play it "cross harp", in a different key from the one marked.
An oboe gives the A for tuning the orchestra because its piercing sound is heard above the other instruments.
Auto-Tune was created in 1997 from seismic analysis techniques used to look for oil.
Spain's national anthem, the Marcha Real, is one of the few anthems in the world with no official lyrics.
A harpsichord cannot play louder or softer with the touch: its strings are plucked by plectra, not struck.
A 100 MHz FM radio wave is about three metres long, which is why car aerials are shorter than medium-wave ones.
Reggae took its name from the song "Do the Reggay" by Toots and the Maytals, from 1968.
Spain's first radio station with regular programming was Radio Barcelona, EAJ-1, opened in November 1924.
A concert grand piano has about 230 strings that together pull with around 20 tonnes of tension on the iron frame.
